title: Businesses Are Using AI to Transform Work, Not Cut Jobs - Liberty Street Economics
gist: The New York Fed's August 2026 Regional Business Surveys of New York and Northern New Jersey firms show AI use jumping to 61 percent of service firms and 51 percent of manufacturers, but adoption is a mile wide and an inch deep: three-quarters of service firms and over 90 percent of manufacturers call their AI spend minimal-to-modest, the median adopter has only 17 percent (services) or 7 percent (manufacturing) of workers using it, and just 4 percent of service firms laid anyone off because of AI. Retraining — roughly a third of service-firm adopters and over 20 percent of manufacturers — remains the dominant workforce response, with entry-level hiring flagged as the one channel where damage may be concentrated.

insights.claim: AI use among New York / Northern New Jersey service firms tracked by the New York Fed's Regional Business Surveys rose from 25 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025 to 61 percent in August 2026, a near-vertical three-year adoption curve.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Diffusion, not experimentation, is now the base case for services — the addressable seat count for AI software vendors is expanding faster than most enterprise-software adoption curves on record.
insights.quote: 61 percent of service firms reported using AI this year, up from 40 percent last year and 25 percent in 2024
insights.locator: AI Adoption Has Become Much More Widespread in the Workplace

insights.claim: Manufacturers in the New York Fed's August 2026 survey reported 51 percent AI use, roughly double the 26 percent of 2025 and triple the 16 percent of 2024 — a steeper relative catch-up than services even though the level remains lower.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: The manufacturing gap is closing fast; industrial-software and factory-floor AI vendors face a market that doubled in twelve months rather than a laggard segment.
insights.quote: roughly double the 26 percent from last year and triple the 16 percent in 2024
insights.locator: Among manufacturers, 51 percent reported using AI

insights.claim: Within services, knowledge-intensive sectors — information, business services, and finance — post the highest AI usage rates of any group in the New York Fed survey.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Concentration in white-collar, knowledge-heavy sectors means productivity and headcount effects should show up first in finance and professional-services cost lines, not in aggregate payrolls.
insights.locator: Businesses in knowledge-intensive sectors

insights.claim: The New York Fed excluded firms that use AI exclusively as an information search tool from its count of AI users, meaning the reported 61 percent and 51 percent adoption rates measure workflow integration rather than casual chatbot lookups.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: A defensible denominator: these numbers are not inflated by 'someone googled with a chatbot,' so cross-study comparisons that use looser definitions will overstate relative adoption elsewhere.
insights.quote: Firms using AI exclusively as an information search tool but nothing else were not counted as AI users.
insights.locator: Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Regional Business Surveys

insights.claim: The New York Fed characterizes its own measured AI adoption shares as toward the high end of the range found in existing studies of workplace AI use, implying regional or methodological factors push these readings above the national consensus.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate a 61 percent service-sector adoption rate to the whole US economy; the NY/NJ region skews knowledge-intensive and is likely a leading, not representative, indicator.
insights.quote: These shares are toward the high end of the range of existing studies of AI use in the workplace.
insights.locator: These shares are toward the high end

themes.theme: Adoption is broad but shallow: spend and seat penetration

insights.claim: Three-quarters of service firms and more than 90 percent of manufacturers surveyed by the New York Fed describe their AI investments as minimal to modest, ranging from free tools to a small share of overall spending.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI monetization at the mid-market level is still tiny relative to adoption headlines — a warning for revenue models that assume broad adoption converts quickly into per-seat spend.
insights.quote: ranging from use of free AI tools to allocating a small share of overall spending to AI tools or services
insights.locator: While AI adoption has become widespread

insights.claim: Only about 15 percent of service firms — and no manufacturers at all — report committing significant resources to AI adoption, with roughly 5 percent of service firms calling it a major strategic investment.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: The real paying customer base is a ~5-15 percent sliver of service firms; the hyperscaler capex story rests on a narrow band of committed buyers, not the broad adopter base.
insights.quote: just 15 percent of service firms—but no manufacturers—indicate they have committed significant resources to AI adoption
insights.locator: Meanwhile, just 15 percent of service firms

insights.claim: Among firms that use AI, the median share of workers actually using it is just 17 percent at service firms and 7 percent at manufacturers, so most adopters have deployed AI to a small minority of their workforce.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Seat penetration, not logo count, is the metric that matters for AI software revenue — and it implies a long runway of expansion revenue if usage deepens, or a stalled cohort if it does not.
insights.locator: Among AI adopters, the median share of workers

insights.claim: Widespread AI adoption at the firm level coexists with limited investment and limited worker usage, meaning headline adoption statistics substantially overstate how much work has actually changed.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Discount adoption-rate headlines when modeling AI-driven productivity or margin effects; the intensity gap is the variable to track quarter over quarter.
insights.quote: In short, AI adoption in the workplace is now fairly broad but investments and worker usage remain limited.
insights.locator: In short, AI adoption in the workplace

themes.theme: Why non-adopters stay out — capability, not cost

insights.claim: Cost was among the least cited reasons non-adopters gave for staying out of AI in the New York Fed's August 2026 survey, undercutting the assumption that price is the main barrier to enterprise AI diffusion.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Price cuts and cheaper inference will not unlock the remaining market; capability and trust improvements will — so watch model quality and governance features rather than token pricing as the adoption lever.
insights.quote: cost does not seem to be the main deterrent—it was among the least cited reasons by non-adopters
insights.locator: Why Businesses Have Not Adopted AI

insights.claim: About half of firms not using AI say the type of work they do simply does not lend itself to the technology, and roughly a quarter say AI is currently not good enough to provide business benefits.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A structural ceiling on the near-term total addressable market: half the holdouts are task-mismatched, which capability gains alone may never convert.
insights.quote: About half of non-adopters said the type of work they do does not lend itself to AI
insights.locator: With AI use in the workplace now widespread

insights.claim: More than a third of AI non-adopters cite data privacy, security, or confidentiality concerns, a similar share cite accuracy or reliability worries, and roughly a third say they lack staff with the technical skills to use AI effectively.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Three separately monetizable gaps — AI security/governance tooling, reliability and evaluation layers, and AI training/implementation services — each addressing roughly a third of the holdout market.
insights.locator: More than a third of non-adopters were concerned

themes.theme: Labor-market impact: layoffs stay rare, hiring drag is the real channel

insights.claim: Only 4 percent of service firms reported laying off workers in response to AI over the past six months, up from 1 percent a year earlier, while no manufacturers reported AI-driven layoffs in either 2025 or 2026.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: AI-attributed layoffs quadrupled off a tiny base — the level is still negligible for macro claims data, but the direction of travel is the thing to re-check in the 2027 survey.
insights.locator: Retraining Remains Common, Layoffs Limited

insights.claim: About 15 percent of service firms said they hired fewer workers than they otherwise would have because of AI, versus 12 percent a year earlier, making suppressed hiring roughly four times as common as outright AI-driven layoffs.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: The AI labor effect shows up in hiring rates and job openings, not initial jobless claims — track JOLTS-style openings and hiring flows rather than layoff announcements for the AI signal.
insights.quote: About 15 percent of service firms said they had hired fewer workers than they would have if not for AI use
insights.locator: About 15 percent of service firms

insights.claim: Roughly 13 percent of service firms hired more workers specifically to help them leverage AI, largely offsetting the 15 percent that hired fewer, so the net headcount effect of AI in the survey is close to a wash.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Net-neutral headcount but heavy compositional churn: the trade is in who gets hired (AI-capable talent) rather than in aggregate employment levels.
insights.locator: However, offsetting these reductions in hiring

insights.claim: No manufacturers increased hiring due to AI in 2026 while a handful reported hiring fewer workers — the first year manufacturers showed any AI-driven hiring reduction, versus none in 2025.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Manufacturing's AI labor effect is turning one-sided — reduction without the offsetting AI-enablement hiring seen in services; an early crack worth monitoring in next year's survey.
insights.locator: A handful of manufacturers reported hiring fewer workers

insights.claim: One recent study cited by the New York Fed finds entry-level workers may be significantly affected because AI substitutes for the routine tasks newer employees perform, potentially raising barriers to workforce entry even as it boosts productivity for experienced workers.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: The distributional risk is concentrated in youth and new-graduate employment, not aggregate payrolls — watch young-worker unemployment and graduate hiring pipelines as the earliest AI displacement tell.
insights.quote: entry-level workers may be affected significantly, as AI can substitute for routine tasks often performed by newer employees, potentially creating barriers to workforce entry
insights.locator: These findings align with the broader research literature

insights.claim: Just over a third of service-firm AI users and more than 20 percent of manufacturing AI users report retraining workers in response to AI, making retraining the single most common workforce adjustment across both sectors.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Corporate-training and workforce-upskilling providers sit in the direct path of AI spend, a less crowded exposure than model or chip layers.
insights.quote: existing workers are much more likely to be retrained than replaced by AI
insights.locator: Consistent with our earlier surveys

insights.claim: Firms report retraining workers across the full educational spectrum in response to AI, though somewhat more of those retrained hold college degrees.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Contradicts the simple 'AI hits the degreed white-collar worker' framing — degree holders are being re-tooled rather than displaced, so wage-premium erosion is not yet the mechanism to underwrite.
insights.locator: Firms report retraining workers across the educational spectrum

insights.claim: Most firms retraining staff for AI focus on helping employees do their current jobs more effectively rather than preparing them for entirely new roles, so AI is being layered onto existing job descriptions instead of restructuring them.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Task-level augmentation, not role redesign, means productivity gains arrive incrementally and slowly — a headwind to near-term margin-expansion stories built on AI.
insights.quote: most firms are focused on helping employees do their current jobs more effectively rather than preparing them for entirely new roles
insights.locator: How Are Businesses Retraining Workers?

insights.claim: Employer AI training clusters into four buckets: basic AI literacy and tool-specific instruction on chatbots and generative AI assistants, automating repetitive tasks, prompt engineering, and job-function-specific AI applications.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A concrete taxonomy for sizing the enterprise AI-enablement market and for judging which vendor claims map to what firms actually buy.
insights.locator: Training falls into several key categories

insights.claim: Concrete deployed use cases reported by surveyed firms include training employees to use AI for marketing and social media content creation, and one firm implementing AI for accounts payable and receivable with human-in-the-loop oversight.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Real production use is landing in marketing content and back-office finance workflows — the near-term revenue pockets for applied AI vendors.
insights.quote: some firms are training employees to use AI for marketing and creating social media content
insights.locator: For example, some firms are training employees

insights.claim: Many companies emphasize responsible AI use in their training — verifying AI outputs, understanding potential biases, following data security protocols, and avoiding over-reliance on the technology.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Verification and governance overhead is a real, unpriced tax on AI productivity gains — and a demand signal for AI assurance, audit, and monitoring tooling.
insights.locator: Notably, many companies emphasized the importance

insights.claim: AI training delivery ranges from formal workshops and external consultants to informal show-and-tell sessions and peer learning, with many organizations relying on encouraged experimentation and hands-on practice rather than structured programs.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: The ad hoc, peer-led delivery model explains the low measured spend and suggests formal AI-training vendors have not yet captured most of this demand.
insights.locator: Delivery methods varied widely

themes.theme: Base case and the conditions that would break it

insights.claim: Three years of New York Fed regional survey data support the conclusion that AI is reshaping the content of work and prompting investment in existing workforces rather than eliminating large numbers of jobs.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: The augmentation-over-replacement base case has Fed survey backing, arguing against positioning for an imminent AI-driven unemployment shock in the near term.
insights.quote: AI has been more likely to augment workers than replace them
insights.locator: Looking Ahead

insights.claim: The New York Fed explicitly flags that AI technology and its applications are still evolving rapidly and that the observed augment-not-replace patterns could shift as adoption matures.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Treat the benign labor reading as a snapshot with an expiry date — the combination of deepening seat penetration and rising capability is the trigger to re-underwrite the displacement thesis.
insights.quote: AI technology and its applications are still evolving rapidly, and these patterns could shift as adoption matures
insights.locator: That said, AI technology and its applications

insights.claim: As AI adoption becomes the norm rather than the exception among regional businesses, retraining has only gained in importance as the primary mechanism through which firms absorb the technology.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Human-capital adaptation, not headcount cuts, is where AI shows up in corporate cost structures right now — an argument for reading SG&A training lines rather than severance charges.
insights.locator: As AI adoption becomes the norm
